[14] In Zeng,6 the Federal Court of Appeal sets out the following test to be applied in determining whether Article 1E of the Convention is applicable in a given case:
Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada's international obligations, and any other relevant facts.

[24] With the greatest respect for the contrary view, the panel cannot agree with such an interpretation for the reasons that follow.

[25] The panel agrees that the Minister only has to prove the claimant's permanent residence on the basis of prima facie evidence, that is, at first glance, in order to have the burden of proof shift to him. However, the evidence submitted by the Minister must personally concern the claimant. In this case, the Minister is instead attempting to unduly extend the application of the reversal of the burden of proof by submitting evidence that is general in nature and completely dissociated from the claimant.

[26] Group determinations can be relevant in refugee law. For example, international law can sometimes incorporate the concept of group determination of refugee status based on prima facie evidence. However, this is a departure from the general principle whereby refugee protection claims must be assessed on an individual basis:
44. While refugee status must normally be determined on an individual basis, situations have also arisen in which entire groups have been displaced under circumstances indicating that members of the group could be considered individually as refugees. In such situations the need to provide assistance is often extremely urgent and it may not be possible for purely practical reasons to carry out an individual determination of refugee status for each member of the group. Recourse has therefore been had to so-called "group determination" of refugee status, whereby each member of the group is regarded prima facie (i.e. in the absence of evidence to the contrary) as a refugee.15

[27] Just as in determining refugee status according to the Convention, the panel must also assess claims submitted under section 97 of the IRPA on an individual basis, according to the very wording of the IRPA.

[28] In other words, the panel must assess a refugee protection claim and render its decision based on the personal circumstances of each claimant. The Minister has provided no reasons as to why a prima facie group determination of permanent resident status should be accepted by the panel in this case to shift the onus to the claimant.

[11] On January 18, 2018, the Minister filed a notice of intervention4 asking the panel to find the claimant to be excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[12] The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of the supporting documentation filed, including a certified true copy of his seized Haitian passport that was on the record.5
Permanent residency in Brazil and exclusion
Test relating to exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention

[13] Article 1E of the Convention states the following:
This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

[14] In Zeng,6 the Federal Court of Appeal sets out the following test to be applied in determining whether Article 1E of the Convention is applicable in a given case:
Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada's international obligations, and any other relevant facts.

[15] Before considering the application of the test to the case at hand, it is important to determine where the burden of proof lies with regard to exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention.
Burden of proof

[16] In his notice of intervention, the Minister states the following, referring to Tajdini7 and Omorogie:8
[translation]
The case law has consistently held that once the Minister has established prima facie that a refugee protection claimant has to be excluded by the application of Article 1E of the Convention, the onus shifts to the claimant to prove lack of status in the third country.9

[17] In fact, once prima facie evidence has been established by the Minister, the reversal of the burden of proof is a principle that is consistently referred to in the case law regarding exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention, in particular since Justice Rothstein's decision in Shahpari,10 then at the Federal Court.
Prima facie evidence and burden of proof reversal

[18] In his notice of intervention, the Minister states:
[translation]
2. According to his statements, the claimant left Haiti on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He then lived in Brazil from December 2014 to June 2016.
3. The claimant's name is on the list of the 43,781 Haitian nationals who were granted permanent residence in Brazil under the Joint Ministerial Order of the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, as published in the Official Union Journal on November 12, 2015.
4. This information makes it possible to establish prima facie evidence that the claimant has permanent resident status in Brazil.
...
13. The Minister argues that he has made a prima facie case that Article 1E of the Refugee Convention applies to the claimant. The evidence on the record demonstrates that the claimant has had access to permanent resident status in Brazil since November 2015.
14. The onus is therefore on the claimant to establish that he no longer has that status in Brazil and/or that he has a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of harm there under subsection 97(1).
15. Furthermore, the documentary evidence shows that in order to be granted permanent residence through that process, the individual in question must fulfil a mere administrative formality.
16. The Minister notes that according to Brazil's Ministry of Labour, approximately 71% of the 43,781 Haitian nationals who were granted permanent residence in Brazil had, in January 2017, completed the steps for obtaining permanent residence through that process.
17. In light of the foregoing, the Minister states that it is more likely than not that the claimant completed this administrative process and that he has permanent resident status in Brazil, giving him rights that are substantially similar to those enjoyed by the nationals of the country.
18. The Minister states that the onus is therefore on the claimant to establish that he does not have such status and to explain the reasons why he did not capitalize on the opportunity under the Joint Ministerial Order of November 2015 to regularize his status in Brazil, when he alleges that he fears returning to his country of origin.11
[translated as it appears in the French version]

[19] For the reasons that follow, the panel does not believe that the elements mentioned above by the Minister are sufficient to establish a prima facie case that the claimant is a permanent resident of Brazil.

[20] Upon reading the joint ministerial order,12 the panel agrees that the 43,781 Haitian nationals on the list must fulfil a mere formality to obtain permanent residence in Brazil. They had one year to do so, that is, until November 2016.

[21] In terms of persecution, the panel must analyze a country of reference as to whether a claimant can acquire by mere formalities the citizenship of that country and that the country does not have discretion to deny citizenship.13 Yet, that principle cannot be transposed when determining whether a claimant must be excluded under Article 1E.

[22] Consequently, a claimant who has not sought to fulfil mere formalities allowing him to acquire the permanent residence of a country cannot be considered a permanent resident for the purposes of exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention.

[23] In addition to the claimant's being on the Brazilian list of November 2015, the Minister notes that 71% of the Haitian nationals on the list completed the required administrative process to be granted permanent residence. He refers to the 31,223 Haitians who had completed the process as of January 2017.14 Again according to the Minister, it would therefore be more likely than not that the claimant, who is on the list, had also completed the process and that he was a permanent resident of Brazil.

[24] With the greatest respect for the contrary view, the panel cannot agree with such an interpretation for the reasons that follow.

[25] The panel agrees that the Minister only has to prove the claimant's permanent residence on the basis of prima facie evidence, that is, at first glance, in order to have the burden of proof shift to him. However, the evidence submitted by the Minister must personally concern the claimant. In this case, the Minister is instead attempting to unduly extend the application of the reversal of the burden of proof by submitting evidence that is general in nature and completely dissociated from the claimant.

[26] Group determinations can be relevant in refugee law. For example, international law can sometimes incorporate the concept of group determination of refugee status based on prima facie evidence. However, this is a departure from the general principle whereby refugee protection claims must be assessed on an individual basis:
44. While refugee status must normally be determined on an individual basis, situations have also arisen in which entire groups have been displaced under circumstances indicating that members of the group could be considered individually as refugees. In such situations the need to provide assistance is often extremely urgent and it may not be possible for purely practical reasons to carry out an individual determination of refugee status for each member of the group. Recourse has therefore been had to so-called "group determination" of refugee status, whereby each member of the group is regarded prima facie (i.e. in the absence of evidence to the contrary) as a refugee.15

[27] Just as in determining refugee status according to the Convention, the panel must also assess claims submitted under section 97 of the IRPA on an individual basis, according to the very wording of the IRPA.

[28] In other words, the panel must assess a refugee protection claim and render its decision based on the personal circumstances of each claimant. The Minister has provided no reasons as to why a prima facie group determination of permanent resident status should be accepted by the panel in this case to shift the onus to the claimant.

[29] The issue here is not a refugee protection claim filed by the group of 43,781 Haitian nationals, but rather by only one of them: the claimant.

[30] To reverse the burden of proof regarding exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention, the Minister must therefore establish a prima facie case that the claimant himself is a permanent resident of Brazil. It is not sufficient to find his name on a list in which most of the people are, to make a prima facie finding that he is, as the Minister does in his notice.

[31] In fact, by way of analogy, if 3 men and 7 women were on a list of 10 people, it is absolutely correct to state that it is more likely than not for a woman to be selected at random from the list. However, if one of the 3 men were selected, it would be completely false to claim that, at first glance, the individual selected must be a woman. Ultimately resorting only to a general statistic without first assessing the evidence relating to the person in question leads to this incongruous result. The refugee protection claimant is not merely a name or a number drawn at random. He is a person with a story, documents and statements, who submitted a refugee protection claim and who deserves that all of the evidence, both general and personal, that concerns him be analyzed with respect to his specific situation. It was incumbent on the Minister to assess the evidence to demonstrate, on a prima facie basis, that the claimant was a permanent resident.

[32] In the absence of other evidence specifically concerning the claimant, for example, through the filing of a residency card or a statement made by the claimant, referring to a general statistic is not usually sufficient to demonstrate the permanent residency of a person, on a prima facie basis. It has not been demonstrated in this case.

[78] The panel acknowledges that elements that are at first glance favourable to the claimant were in fact removed. However, it cannot accept counsel's argument. In fact, as mentioned above, the false content of the story had been signed by the claimant and filed into evidence by him knowingly. Removing a few false elements, which could have helped the claimant's cause had they been maintained, is a small price to pay for the final version of the story to be more intelligible and coherent. In any case, the claimant must be able to credibly explain the major amendments he made, regardless of whether the result in the final version of his story is positive or negative for him. And yet, he failed to do so.

[79] The claimant filed the death certificate of a woman named XXXX XXXX.35 However, in both his BOC Form and his background form,36 the claimant states that his mother was named XXXX XXXX, not XXXX XXXX XXXX The birth certificate and the extract from the birth certificate registry list XXXX XXXX as his mother. Even assuming that the three names designate the same person, namely, his mother, the death certificate at best shows that his mother passed away on November 27, 2011, in Fonds-Parisien around 7:00 p.m., without providing any details regarding the cause or causes of her death.
CONCLUSION

[80] After analyzing all of the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant has not discharged his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds. He also failed to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, should he return to Haiti, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[78] The panel acknowledges that elements that are at first glance favourable to the claimant were in fact removed. However, it cannot accept counsel's argument. In fact, as mentioned above, the false content of the story had been signed by the claimant and filed into evidence by him knowingly. Removing a few false elements, which could have helped the claimant's cause had they been maintained, is a small price to pay for the final version of the story to be more intelligible and coherent. In any case, the claimant must be able to credibly explain the major amendments he made, regardless of whether the result in the final version of his story is positive or negative for him. And yet, he failed to do so.

[79] The claimant filed the death certificate of a woman named XXXX XXXX.35 However, in both his BOC Form and his background form,36 the claimant states that his mother was named XXXX XXXX, not XXXX XXXX XXXX The birth certificate and the extract from the birth certificate registry list XXXX XXXX as his mother. Even assuming that the three names designate the same person, namely, his mother, the death certificate at best shows that his mother passed away on November 27, 2011, in Fonds-Parisien around 7:00 p.m., without providing any details regarding the cause or causes of her death.
CONCLUSION

[80] After analyzing all of the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant has not discharged his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds. He also failed to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, should he return to Haiti, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[81] For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection," and rejects his refugee protection claim.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] The refugee protection claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Haiti. He alleges that he is a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
ALLEGATIONS
[2] In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form),1 as amended on January 16, 2018,2 the claimant alleges the following.

[3] A group of thugs wanted to kill the claimant's older brother because of an unpaid debt. On November 27, 2011, the thugs went to the claimant's home and began throwing rocks. He called the police, but they never showed up. The claimant's brother escaped through a window. The thugs then entered the house and stated that they would watch the house until they captured their debtor, who decided not to return home.
[4] Later in the afternoon, the group of thugs returned to the house, looking for the claimant's brother. Having not found him, they killed the claimant's mother, who was alone in the house.

[5] The claimant's brother arrived in Brazil on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Realizing that they would not get their hands on his brother, the thugs went to kill the claimant's father on February 6, 2014, then decided to kill each family member, one after another. The claimant hid in the forest for several months until he left Haiti for the Dominican Republic on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He then left for Brazil and arrived there on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

[6] He found work a few days later on January 27, 2015. However, he started being discriminated against at work. His supervisor ordered him to work but paid him a daily salary rather than an hourly rate; he was paid $30 for 12 hours worked, instead of $64 for 8 hours, as was done before Brazil's economic crisis. His colleagues also made prejudicial comments about his race and Haitian nationality.

[7] The claimant was laid off by his employer on March 20, 2016, because of the national crisis, when it was nearly impossible to find work in Brazil. The claimant thus considered leaving that country for the United States, which he did on June 15, 2016. After travelling through eight countries over six months, he arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Being unable to work or to receive social assistance in the United States and not having money to pay a lawyer to claim asylum, he left for Canada, where he arrived on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. His claim was received on July 25, 2017.

[8] The morning of February 2, 2018, a new and substantial amendment was filed by the claimant in the hearing room.3 In it, he names people he fears in Haiti; explains that his brother had money that did not belong to him stolen, resulting in the unpaid debt; indicates that the thugs had come once, not twice on November 27, 2011; and provides details as to how he fled from his home in the company of his brother. He also mentions that the thugs had gone to where he was, that is, the Dominican Republic, with the intention of killing him, whereas his brother was in Brazil.
DETERMINATION

[9] Considering the claimant's lack of credibility, the panel determines that he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" for the reasons set out below.
MINISTER'S INTERVENTION

[10] On January 5, 2018, the Refugee Protection Division (hereinafter the "RPD") sent a notice to the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship of Canada (hereinafter the "Minister") concerning the possibility that Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (hereinafter the "Convention") applies to the claimant because of possible permanent residency in Brazil.

[11] On January 18, 2018, the Minister filed a notice of intervention4 asking the panel to find the claimant to be excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[12] The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of the supporting documentation filed, including a certified true copy of his seized Haitian passport that was on the record.5
Permanent residency in Brazil and exclusion
Test relating to exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention

[13] Article 1E of the Convention states the following:
This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.

[14] In Zeng,6 the Federal Court of Appeal sets out the following test to be applied in determining whether Article 1E of the Convention is applicable in a given case:
Considering all relevant factors to the date of the hearing, does the claimant have status, substantially similar to that of its nationals, in the third country? If the answer is yes, the claimant is excluded. If the answer is no, the next question is whether the claimant previously had such status and lost it, or had access to such status and failed to acquire it. If the answer is no, the claimant is not excluded under Article 1E. If the answer is yes, the RPD must consider and balance various factors. These include, but are not limited to, the reason for the loss of status (voluntary or involuntary), whether the claimant could return to the third country, the risk the claimant would face in the home country, Canada's international obligations, and any other relevant facts.

[15] Before considering the application of the test to the case at hand, it is important to determine where the burden of proof lies with regard to exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention.
Burden of proof

[16] In his notice of intervention, the Minister states the following, referring to Tajdini7 and Omorogie:8
[translation]
The case law has consistently held that once the Minister has established prima facie that a refugee protection claimant has to be excluded by the application of Article 1E of the Convention, the onus shifts to the claimant to prove lack of status in the third country.9

[17] In fact, once prima facie evidence has been established by the Minister, the reversal of the burden of proof is a principle that is consistently referred to in the case law regarding exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention, in particular since Justice Rothstein's decision in Shahpari,10 then at the Federal Court.
Prima facie evidence and burden of proof reversal

[18] In his notice of intervention, the Minister states:
[translation]
2. According to his statements, the claimant left Haiti on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He then lived in Brazil from December 2014 to June 2016.
3. The claimant's name is on the list of the 43,781 Haitian nationals who were granted permanent residence in Brazil under the Joint Ministerial Order of the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare, as published in the Official Union Journal on November 12, 2015.
4. This information makes it possible to establish prima facie evidence that the claimant has permanent resident status in Brazil.
...
13. The Minister argues that he has made a prima facie case that Article 1E of the Refugee Convention applies to the claimant. The evidence on the record demonstrates that the claimant has had access to permanent resident status in Brazil since November 2015.
14. The onus is therefore on the claimant to establish that he no longer has that status in Brazil and/or that he has a well-founded fear of persecution or risk of harm there under subsection 97(1).
15. Furthermore, the documentary evidence shows that in order to be granted permanent residence through that process, the individual in question must fulfil a mere administrative formality.
16. The Minister notes that according to Brazil's Ministry of Labour, approximately 71% of the 43,781 Haitian nationals who were granted permanent residence in Brazil had, in January 2017, completed the steps for obtaining permanent residence through that process.
17. In light of the foregoing, the Minister states that it is more likely than not that the claimant completed this administrative process and that he has permanent resident status in Brazil, giving him rights that are substantially similar to those enjoyed by the nationals of the country.
18. The Minister states that the onus is therefore on the claimant to establish that he does not have such status and to explain the reasons why he did not capitalize on the opportunity under the Joint Ministerial Order of November 2015 to regularize his status in Brazil, when he alleges that he fears returning to his country of origin.11
[translated as it appears in the French version]

[19] For the reasons that follow, the panel does not believe that the elements mentioned above by the Minister are sufficient to establish a prima facie case that the claimant is a permanent resident of Brazil.

[20] Upon reading the joint ministerial order,12 the panel agrees that the 43,781 Haitian nationals on the list must fulfil a mere formality to obtain permanent residence in Brazil. They had one year to do so, that is, until November 2016.

[21] In terms of persecution, the panel must analyze a country of reference as to whether a claimant can acquire by mere formalities the citizenship of that country and that the country does not have discretion to deny citizenship.13 Yet, that principle cannot be transposed when determining whether a claimant must be excluded under Article 1E.

[22] Consequently, a claimant who has not sought to fulfil mere formalities allowing him to acquire the permanent residence of a country cannot be considered a permanent resident for the purposes of exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention.

[23] In addition to the claimant's being on the Brazilian list of November 2015, the Minister notes that 71% of the Haitian nationals on the list completed the required administrative process to be granted permanent residence. He refers to the 31,223 Haitians who had completed the process as of January 2017.14 Again according to the Minister, it would therefore be more likely than not that the claimant, who is on the list, had also completed the process and that he was a permanent resident of Brazil.
[24] With the greatest respect for the contrary view, the panel cannot agree with such an interpretation for the reasons that follow.

[25] The panel agrees that the Minister only has to prove the claimant's permanent residence on the basis of prima facie evidence, that is, at first glance, in order to have the burden of proof shift to him. However, the evidence submitted by the Minister must personally concern the claimant. In this case, the Minister is instead attempting to unduly extend the application of the reversal of the burden of proof by submitting evidence that is general in nature and completely dissociated from the claimant.

[26] Group determinations can be relevant in refugee law. For example, international law can sometimes incorporate the concept of group determination of refugee status based on prima facie evidence. However, this is a departure from the general principle whereby refugee protection claims must be assessed on an individual basis:
44. While refugee status must normally be determined on an individual basis, situations have also arisen in which entire groups have been displaced under circumstances indicating that members of the group could be considered individually as refugees. In such situations the need to provide assistance is often extremely urgent and it may not be possible for purely practical reasons to carry out an individual determination of refugee status for each member of the group. Recourse has therefore been had to so-called "group determination" of refugee status, whereby each member of the group is regarded prima facie (i.e. in the absence of evidence to the contrary) as a refugee.15

[27] Just as in determining refugee status according to the Convention, the panel must also assess claims submitted under section 97 of the IRPA on an individual basis, according to the very wording of the IRPA.

[28] In other words, the panel must assess a refugee protection claim and render its decision based on the personal circumstances of each claimant. The Minister has provided no reasons as to why a prima facie group determination of permanent resident status should be accepted by the panel in this case to shift the onus to the claimant.
[29] The issue here is not a refugee protection claim filed by the group of 43,781 Haitian nationals, but rather by only one of them: the claimant.

[30] To reverse the burden of proof regarding exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention, the Minister must therefore establish a prima facie case that the claimant himself is a permanent resident of Brazil. It is not sufficient to find his name on a list in which most of the people are, to make a prima facie finding that he is, as the Minister does in his notice.

[31] In fact, by way of analogy, if 3 men and 7 women were on a list of 10 people, it is absolutely correct to state that it is more likely than not for a woman to be selected at random from the list. However, if one of the 3 men were selected, it would be completely false to claim that, at first glance, the individual selected must be a woman. Ultimately resorting only to a general statistic without first assessing the evidence relating to the person in question leads to this incongruous result. The refugee protection claimant is not merely a name or a number drawn at random. He is a person with a story, documents and statements, who submitted a refugee protection claim and who deserves that all of the evidence, both general and personal, that concerns him be analyzed with respect to his specific situation. It was incumbent on the Minister to assess the evidence to demonstrate, on a prima facie basis, that the claimant was a permanent resident.

[32] In the absence of other evidence specifically concerning the claimant, for example, through the filing of a residency card or a statement made by the claimant, referring to a general statistic is not usually sufficient to demonstrate the permanent residency of a person, on a prima facie basis. It has not been demonstrated in this case.

[33] All of the case law noted by the panel regarding the reversal of the burden of proof in the context of exclusion under Article 1E of the Convention includes evidence of permanent residence directly concerning the personal situation of the claimants in question. A sampling of the unanimous case law is cited below.

[34] At issue in Shahpari16 are the valid permanent resident cards of the applicants at the time of the hearing:
The evidence advanced by the respondent demonstrates that the applicants' carte de resident was valid at the time of the hearing, that the only obligation of a holder of a carte was "to avoid breaking the law" of which there was no evidence, and that if a holder of a carte was outside France for more than 3 years, the holder must re-apply for a carte de resident.
[35] The cards belonged to the respondents and therefore reflected their personal status.

[36] In Choovak,17 several elements, all of them specific to the applicant in question, tended to demonstrate her permanent resident status:
It is submitted that the respondent held a German travel document that indicated her residency status in Germany was unlimited or unrestricted ("unbefristet") or that the respondent was a permanent resident of Germany. This Residence Permit also included the following supplementary provision: "Gainful employment requiring a work permit permitted only in accordance with a valid work permit". Furthermore, when the respondent applied for a student visa to enter Canada, she allegedly indicated in her visitor's visa application that her residence permit was for an "indefinite period" and expired on December 31, 2000. A Canadian Immigration Program Manager in Berlin, responding to a request for information, would also have indicated to her that although the validity of her status was until December 31, 2000, "this would be extended upon application". The FOSS notes of the respondent's interview for her student visa further indicate that the respondent told the Immigration Officer that she had permanent residence in Germany and that she intended to study medicine in Germany after returning from Canada.18
[the panel's emphasis]

[37] In his analysis, Justice Rouleau considered the numerous pieces of evidence cited in the above extract. Of those, he notes the evidence reproduced in bold font to establish that there is prima facie proof of permanent residence:
There is in fact prima facie proof in the terms of the German travel gray document and in the terms of the residence permit which had been issued that the respondent had permanent resident status subject to a renewal every two years.19
[38] Again, a travel document and a resident permit issued to the applicant concern her personal situation.

[39] In Nepete, after citing Justice Rothstein in Shahpari regarding the reversal of the burden of proof, Justice Henegan states that the Minister met the obligation by producing a letter.20 The content of the letter is described in the judgment:

[9] In reaching its conclusion, the Board relied upon a letter received from the Consulate General of the Czech Republic in Montreal. This letter, dated July 13, 1999, was entered as exhibit R4 at the hearing before the Board. This letter, addressed to the Board, confirms that the Applicant had been granted a permanent residence permit in the Czech Republic on October 29, 1994 for family reunion purposes, following his marriage with a Czech citizen on June 20, 1987. His status as a permanent resident was unaffected by his subsequent divorce on October 7, 1997.

[10] The letter advises that the Applicant's permanent residence is still registered at a street address in the Czech Republic. Furthermore, this letter advises that due to the expiry of his re-entry visa, the Applicant cannot automatically re-enter the Czech Republic but must apply for a visa from that country.21
[40] Once more, the letter in that case specifically addresses the applicant's situation.
[41] In Hussein Ramadan,22 Justice Tremblay-Lamer states:

[21] In its decision, the panel was of the opinion that in light of the documentary and testimonial evidence, a prima facie case was established that the applicant met the criteria of Article 1E of the Convention.

[22] The panel took into consideration the information provided by the applicant in her Personal Information Form, in which she stated that she had permanent residence status in Paraguay. The panel also relied on the applicant's testimony at the hearing that she had had permanent residence status since 1996 and on the objective evidence that permanent residence in Paraguay grants a right to stay in the country indefinitely.

[23] Considering that evidence and the case law, the panel found that a prima facie case had been established that on the day the hearing finished, February 9, 2010, the claimant had "the right to return to her country of residence, the right to work there freely without restrictions, the right to study there and the right to access the social services in Paraguay with no restrictions other than those that apply to Paraguayan citizens".

[24] The panel's finding that there was prima facie evidence that the applicant was still a permanent resident of Paraguay was made on the basis of objective and credible evidence, and the Court must afford the panel deference.23

[42] That case concerned both oral and written statements made by the applicant that she was a permanent resident. In Dieng,24 Justice de Montigny also notes the applicants' statements regarding their own status, finding that there was prima facie evidence.25 In Mikelaj, Justice Elliott finds that the applicant failed to rebut the prima facie evidence:26 the "Italian authorities indicated the Applicant was a permanent resident of Italy whose permit was still valid and had no expiry date."27 Once again, the evidence directly concerned the person in question.

[43] Considering all of the foregoing and the lack of evidence that specifically concerns him, the burden of proof should not shift to the claimant for his merely being on the list of the Brazilian ministerial order of November 2015, even when there is evidence that 71% of the people on that list acquired permanent residence in Brazil.
Is the claimant a permanent resident of Brazil on a balance of probabilities?

[44] Although the panel found that the claimant's being on the Brazilian list and the overall statistic applying to 71% of the Haitians on that list are not in themselves sufficient to reverse the burden of proof, it must analyze all of the evidence, including the claimant's testimony at the hearing, in order to determine whether the claimant is, on a balance of probabilities, a permanent resident who essentially has the same rights and obligations as Brazilian nationals.

[45] The claimant stated in his testimony that he arrived in Brazil on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and that he left that country on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He apparently received a protocol from the Brazilian authorities on December 24, 2014. In January 2016, his work permit had expired and he allegedly went to the federal police, who stamped his papers. He was also issued a CPF card by the Brazilian government.28 He stated that he had never had a foreigner identity card, namely, the residence card.

[46] With respect to his rights and obligations, he testified that he had the right to go to school, to legally work, to access Brazil's public healthcare system, but that he did not have the right to return to Brazil, because he did not have a card.
[47] In his background form29 and generic application form,30 he states having been a temporary resident of Brazil from December 2014 to June 2016.

[48] Furthermore, although the panel rejects the claimant's testimony as non-credible for the reasons set out below, the evidence includes an objective element noted by the panel that is not based on the claimant's word.

[49] In fact, the claimant called the Embassy of Brazil in Canada the day before the hearing in an attempt to demonstrate his Brazilian status. The panel noted in the hearing room, by examining the claimant's cell phone, that a call had been made to the number corresponding to that embassy 21 hours before the hearing. The claimant's counsel also spontaneously offered that the panel examine his own telephone, which had been used the day after the claimant's cell phone had lost the signal and which showed that a call of 5 minutes and 42 seconds had been made to the same number.

[50] Despite the claimant's lack of credibility discussed below, it is objectively verifiable that a call was made to the Embassy of Brazil in Canada before the hearing. Although the lateness of this initiative, that is, the day before the hearing, casts doubt on the concrete results that the claimant would have hoped to achieve by taking such a step before the hearing, the panel gives him the benefit of the doubt regarding only this aspect, considering that he also provided his CPF card and that he had stated upon his entry in the country that he was a temporary resident of Brazil.

[51] Considering all of the foregoing, the panel finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a permanent resident of Brazil.
Credibility

[52] The panel noted contradictions in the explanations provided by the claimant to explain the extensive changes made to his BOC Form. Those contradictions and the omission of several important elements missing from the previous versions of his account, were not explained to the panel's satisfaction, which undermines the claimant's credibility. Consequently, the panel rejects all of his testimony.

[53] The claimant amended nearly his entire account through two amendments. By counting the crossed out passages and the passages added, the final version consists of 113 lines, of which barely 20 are completely free of additions, modifications or deletions with respect to the initial version of the claimant's account.

[54] The first amendment31 is dated January 16, 2018, and was received on January 22, 2018. The second amendment32 is dated February 1, 2018, and was received in the hearing room by the panel just before the start of the hearing held on February 2, 2018.

[55] At the hearing, the claimant explained that he had his original account translated by someone at the YMCA. He added that he thought that his counsel at the time, Mr. Karkar, was going to correct his story before submitting it, but in the end, he had not made any corrections.

[56] When the panel asked him what role the interpreter working with Mr. Karkar had played with respect to his original BOC Form, the claimant replied that he did not have an interpreter. The panel then pointed out to the claimant that his BOC Form indicates that Jean Loubens Carius had served as interpreter. The claimant answered no interpreter had sat next to him to provide him with any explanation.
[57] Later during the hearing, the claimant testified that the immigration authorities had informed him that Mr. Karkar could no longer argue cases as a member of the Bar.

[58] Again according to his oral testimony, the first amendment dated January 16, 2018, was allegedly prepared when the claimant had gone to the office of his current counsel, when the latter was not there and with only an interpreter and the counsel's secretary present. The interpreter had apparently told him that, because the first version of his account had been sent to the immigration authorities and that it contained errors, she could not see any major corrections to be made, only small details. Later during the hearing, he specified that the interpreter had told him that she could not modify the document, because it had already been sent to immigration. She reportedly stated that she could make small changes.

[59] It was only the day before the hearing that the claimant, through his second amendment, had modified his account in the presence of his counsel, because the latter had told him that he did not understand the translation and that the words made no sense and were incoherent.
[60] For the following reasons, the panel cannot accept this version of the facts as justification for the substantial amendments made by the claimant.

[61] First, the claimant claims that, for the first amendment in January 2018, the interpreter had wanted to make only small changes, because the account had already been submitted to the immigration authorities. Yet, upon reading that first amended version of the account, the changes are far from minor.

[62] In fact, following the amendment made by an interpreter who supposedly wanted to make only small changes, the claimant's date of birth was corrected, the call to the police on November 24, 2011, and the home invasion during which the claimant's mother was killed on November 27, 2011, had now occurred the same day, racist comments had now been made by his work colleagues rather than his supervisor, the passage in which he states that he had been harassed daily by Brazilians in the neighbourhood where he lived was crossed out, as was the one in which he states that he was becoming a target of mockery and scorn and the one in which he states that Brazilians had threatened and spit on him.

[63] In addition, the first amendment was signed not only by the claimant, but also by the interpreter, under the following statement:
[translation]
I CERTIFY that I have a good knowledge of the Creole and French languages and that I provided the refugee protection claimant with as faithful an oral translation as possible of this amendment. Dated in Montréal, this 16th day of January in 2018."33

[64] So, according to a document signed by the claimant and submitted into evidence by him, he had also apparently received an oral translation of the amendment. Yet, at the hearing, he contradicted that statement, testifying that the first amendment to his BOC Form had not been translated for him by the interpreter.
[65] When the panel asked him to explain why his testimony contradicted the interpreter's statement, he replied that her making the amendments with him was in the story.

[66] Because his response in no way answered the question, he was asked the question again. The claimant then stated that the night before, his lawyer had explained to him what was in the amendment, and as for the interpreter, it was in his story that she had been with him and that there were errors in it. He added that it was the original translator who had made the errors. At best, that confusing response only reiterates the justifications alleged by the claimant regarding his major amendments, without in any way explaining why he had just contradicted his own evidence.

[67] When the panel asked the claimant whether the name of the interpreter listed in the first amendment was indeed the name of the interpreter who had been with him, he replied that it was not. Counsel spontaneously intervened, stating that it was indeed the interpreter whose name was in the amendment of January 2018, thereby contradicting his client.

[68] When the panel asked the claimant why he had answered no when the document and his counsel indicated that it was the right person, the claimant replied that he had not clearly understood the interpreter's name. Yet, the panel's question was clear and simple and both the claimant and the interpreter at the hearing confirmed that they clearly understood each other. Furthermore, the claimant was at liberty to ask that the question, or even just the name be repeated if he had not clearly understood it, especially when it was the name of one of the people allegedly responsible for his predicament.

[69] The panel also asked the claimant to explain why the theft of which his brother had been a victim was completely omitted from his original account and from his amended account of January 2018, and mentioned only in the final version. The panel also confronted the claimant with another major omission, such as the allegation that the thugs had wanted to go to the Dominican Republic to get him or even that the story differed completely with respect to interactions with the thugs, when he called the police and when the thugs had allegedly gone to the house twice in a single day, rather than once. Each time, he basically replied that he had told the right story, but the translators had made errors.

[70] However, in order to accept that explanation and the claimant's version of the facts, one would have to accept that the claimant had not only fallen on a former counsel who was currently disbarred, which the panel does not question, but also on an initial incompetent translator who made errors, then on another interpreter who, like the claimant, signed his original BOC Form without having interpreted it. One would also have to accept that he then fell on a dishonest interpreter in the office of his current counsel, with respect to the first amendment in January 2018, who had supposedly chosen, in the claimant's place, the changes to be made to the account that he himself signed and who had told him that she could make only minor changes when, in fact, she made major changes, as mentioned above, and who then signed a false statement that she translated the amendment for the claimant orally, thereby shooting herself in the foot, because in doing so, she would have thus risked her reputation and client base by undermining the case of the claimant and his counsel.

[71] Furthermore, the claimant's version of the facts suggests that both the original translator and the interpreter in January 2018 respectively either made a mistake or refused to amend elements that were both critical and uncomplicated, such as the simple allegation that the problems of the claimant and his brother stem from theft of the money borrowed by the latter in Croix-des-Bouquets, or even that the thugs had gone all the way to the Dominican Republic to get him, thereby revealing how dangerous they were and their motivation. Yet, according to the claimant, both of the interpreters apparently ignored those allegations.

[72] What is more, when taking the claimant's explanations at face value, they suggest that the interpreter in January 2018 would have explained to the claimant that the amendment ultimately included only minor changes, because she could not make major amendments, because the account had already been submitted to the immigration authorities, and that he had recounted his story correctly for her. Knowing that, the claimant not only signed the amendment, knowing it to be false, but also submitted it into evidence.34 In addition, in response to a question from his counsel as to why several lines had been crossed out in the last version of his story, he stated that everything written there was false. Yet, nearly all of those lines are included in the amendment of January 2018.

[73] Considering all of the foregoing, the panel does not believe the claimant's explanations regarding the extensive and major amendments made to his account or the significant elements that were initially omitted from his original and amended stories. His credibility is fatally undermined, thereby rendering his testimony non-credible.
[74] All of the claimant's non-credible testimony leads the panel to believe nothing of his story of persecution, risks and threats.

[75] In his submissions, the claimant's counsel notes that the story of a refugee protection claimant must not be viewed as an indelible mark. Rather, he argues that a claimant has the right to make any reasonable modification prior to the hearing so as to ensure that the record is up-to-date and truthful.

[76] The panel fully agrees with the overall position of counsel. However, the claimant's explanations justifying the major amendments to the basis of his refugee protection claim prior to the hearing must be credible, which is not the claimant's case here for the above-mentioned reasons.

[77] Counsel also argued that he was aware that the last version of his client's story included major amendments, but that many elements that had never been stated by the claimant had ultimately been removed, despite the fact that keeping them in the story would have favoured his client. For example, counsel pointed out that the statement that the claimant had called the police, but that the police did not come, had been removed because it was false, even though it would have tended to demonstrate that state protection was ineffective.

[78] The panel acknowledges that elements that are at first glance favourable to the claimant were in fact removed. However, it cannot accept counsel's argument. In fact, as mentioned above, the false content of the story had been signed by the claimant and filed into evidence by him knowingly. Removing a few false elements, which could have helped the claimant's cause had they been maintained, is a small price to pay for the final version of the story to be more intelligible and coherent. In any case, the claimant must be able to credibly explain the major amendments he made, regardless of whether the result in the final version of his story is positive or negative for him. And yet, he failed to do so.

[79] The claimant filed the death certificate of a woman named XXXX XXXX.35 However, in both his BOC Form and his background form,36 the claimant states that his mother was named XXXX XXXX, not XXXX XXXX XXXX The birth certificate and the extract from the birth certificate registry list XXXX XXXX as his mother. Even assuming that the three names designate the same person, namely, his mother, the death certificate at best shows that his mother passed away on November 27, 2011, in Fonds-Parisien around 7:00 p.m., without providing any details regarding the cause or causes of her death.
CONCLUSION

[80] After analyzing all of the evidence, the panel finds that the claimant has not discharged his burden of establishing that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds. He also failed to demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, should he return to Haiti, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

[81] For all these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection," and rejects his refugee protection claim.
